# Gen-1 Subclass Error Analysis by Generator

Binary LOGO evaluation (gen-1 vs gen-2+), with per-generator error breakdown sorted by model size.

## Results

| Generator | Size | gen-1 N | gen-1 F1 | FNR | FPR | Macro-F1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-0.6B | 0.6B | 986 | 0.6684 | 0.2353 | 0.2019 | 0.7568 |
| OLMo-2-1B | 1.0B | 988 | 0.6077 | 0.1549 | 0.3388 | 0.6889 |
| Pythia-1B | 1.0B | 993 | 0.7200 | 0.1712 | 0.1831 | 0.7938 |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 1.7B | 983 | 0.6764 | 0.1475 | 0.2491 | 0.7540 |
| Pythia-2.8B | 2.8B | 989 | 0.6718 | 0.1112 | 0.2853 | 0.7427 |
| Llama-3.2-3B | 3.0B | 984 | 0.6207 | 0.0711 | 0.3876 | 0.6841 |
| Mistral-7B-v0.3 | 7.0B | 994 | 0.5097 | 0.0644 | 0.6034 | 0.5344 |
| Qwen3-8B | 8.0B | 979 | 0.6008 | 0.0776 | 0.4455 | 0.6503 |

- FNR = gen-1 misclassified as gen-2+ (false negative rate for gen-1 class)
- FPR = gen-2+ misclassified as gen-1 (false positive rate for gen-1 class)

## Spearman Correlations (model size vs metric)

| Metric | rho | p-value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| size vs FNR | -0.9222 | 0.0011 |
| size vs gen-1 F1 | -0.5868 | 0.1262 |
| size vs FPR | +0.8383 | 0.0093 |

## Key Findings

1. **FPR increases with model size (rho=+0.84, p=0.009)**: Gen-2+ outputs from larger models are frequently misclassified as gen-1. Mistral-7B has FPR=0.60 (60% of its gen-2+ is confused with gen-1) vs Pythia-1B at FPR=0.18. This directly supports the "larger models compress depth margins" claim: subsequent generation passes through a larger model fail to accumulate the statistical fingerprint that distinguishes gen-2+ from gen-1.

2. **FNR decreases with model size (rho=-0.92, p=0.001)**: Gen-1 from larger models is rarely misclassified as gen-2+. Mistral-7B has FNR=0.06 vs Qwen3-0.6B at FNR=0.24. Larger models produce a distinctive gen-1 fingerprint (one pass away from human text), but further passes do not deepen the signal proportionally.

3. **Mechanistic interpretation**: Smaller models add substantial incremental distortion at each depth, making gen-1 vs gen-2+ separable. Larger models apply a strong but saturating transformation: the first pass creates a clear fingerprint, but additional passes add negligible further drift, compressing the gen-1/gen-2+ margin.

## Method
- Classifier: sklearn HistGradientBoostingClassifier (max_iter=200, max_depth=6, lr=0.1)
- Evaluation: 8-generator Leave-One-Generator-Out binary (gen-1=0, gen-2+=1, gen-0 excluded)
- Downsampled training to balanced classes per fold
- Features: entropy_mean/std/min/max, tail_decay, ttr, hapax_ratio

# Corpus Prevalence Estimation Demo

## Setup
- 5 synthetic corpora: 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% depth-2+ proportion
- Corpus size: 800 documents each
- 8 held-out generators (LOGO), 200 bootstrap resamples per corpus
- 4 quantification methods: CC, ACC, PCC, EMQ

## Results

| True depth-2+ % | EMQ Predicted % | |Error| | 95% CI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0% | 2.3% | 2.34pp | [1.0%, 4.1%] |
| 25% | 27.1% | 8.87pp | [23.7%, 30.7%] |
| 50% | 49.7% | 11.70pp | [45.8%, 53.7%] |
| 75% | 71.2% | 13.20pp | [67.0%, 75.3%] |
| 100% | 88.8% | 11.16pp | [85.9%, 91.6%] |

## Method Comparison (MAE across 5 corpora, 8 generators)

| Method | MAE |
| --- | --- |
| CC (Classify & Count) | 16.96pp |
| ACC (Adjusted CC) | 11.19pp |
| PCC (Probabilistic CC) | 19.34pp |
| EMQ (EM Quantification) | 9.45pp |

## Per-Generator EMQ Performance (MAE across 5 corpora)

| Generator | EMQ MAE | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pythia-2.8b | ~1.1pp | Excellent calibration |
| olmo-2-1b | ~3.5pp | Good |
| llama-3.2-3b | ~6.6pp | Moderate |
| qwen3-1.7b | ~6.4pp | Moderate |
| pythia-1b | ~7.6pp | Moderate |
| mistral-7b-v0.3 | ~12.4pp | Poor (high domain shift) |
| qwen3-0.6b | ~11.3pp | Poor |
| qwen3-8b | ~12.3pp | Poor |

## Conclusion

MAE = 9.45pp (best, EMQ) >= 5pp threshold.

**Corpus-level depth auditing is NOT viable in the strict LOGO (cross-generator) setting** with the current 7-feature XGBoost classifier.

Key observations:
1. For in-distribution generators (pythia-2.8b, olmo-2-1b), MAE < 3.5pp, demonstrating the method is sound when domain shift is small.
2. The bottleneck is generator-specific domain shift in LOGO, not the quantification method itself.
3. EMQ (Saerens et al. 2002) provides the best correction by adapting posterior probabilities to the test distribution without explicit TPR/FPR estimation.
4. Naive classify-and-count systematically underestimates high proportions and overestimates low proportions (regression to the mean).

## Outputs
- Plot: `/root/gen-depth-fingerprint/results/corpus_prevalence_calibration.pdf`
- Data: `/root/gen-depth-fingerprint/results/corpus_prevalence_demo.json`
- Script: `/root/gen-depth-fingerprint/corpus_prevalence_demo.py`
- Log: `/root/gen-depth-fingerprint/logs/corpus_prevalence_demo.log`

# Pareto Throughput Analysis

Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5090 32 GB, FP16, avg sequence length ~237 tokens, N=100 texts.

## Throughput vs. Accuracy

| Method | ms/text | Binary F1 | 3-class F1 | Pareto | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LD-Score | 0.61 | 0.6788 | 0.6326 | Yes | CPU trigram JSD, no GPU model |
| AvgLogProb | 8.58 | 0.6785 | 0.7085 | | 1x Pythia-410M forward |
| FastDetectGPT | 8.58 | 0.5805 | 0.6654 | | 1x Pythia-410M forward (shared) |
| **7-Feature (Ours)** | **9.70** | **0.6935** | **0.7616** | **Yes** | 1x Pythia-410M + CPU features + XGBoost |
| Binoculars | 22.17 | 0.5327 | 0.4094 | | 1x 410M + 1x 1B forward |
| 4-Det Ensemble | 22.80 | 0.6993 | 0.7790 | Yes | 4 detectors, shared 410M pass + 1B |
| 4-Det+Surface | 22.80 | 0.7044 | 0.7823 | Yes | 4 detectors + TTR + hapax_ratio |

## Key Findings

- **7-Feature is 2.4x faster** than 4-Det+Surface (9.7 vs 22.8 ms/text) with only 1.5% relative F1 gap (0.6935 vs 0.7044).
- **7-Feature sits on the Pareto frontier**: no method achieves both higher F1 and lower latency.
- **Resource efficiency**: 7-Feature uses 1 model (410M params, 905 MB GPU) vs 4-Det's 2 models (1.41B params, 2868 MB GPU), a 3.2x memory reduction.
- **LD-Score** is the fastest method (0.61 ms, CPU-only) with competitive binary F1, but its 3-class F1 (0.6326) is far below 7-Feature (0.7616), showing it cannot discriminate generation depth.
- **FLOPs ratio**: 7-Feature uses 1.94e+11 FLOPs/text vs 4-Det's 6.68e+11 (optimized), a 3.4x reduction.

## Output

- Figure: `artifacts/_project/paper/chart/fig_appendix_pareto.pdf`
- Data source: `results/efficiency_comparison.json` + `results/8gen_baselines.json`

## Experiment

**Goal**: Address the seed-sharing confound. For each (seed, generator), subtract depth-0 feature values as a baseline, then classify gen-1 vs gen-2+ using only the delta features.

**Data**: 37058 total rows -> 29095 after removing depth-0.

## Results

| Generator | Binary F1 | 95% CI |
|-----------|-----------|--------|
| pythia-1b | 0.7814 | [0.7664, 0.7967] |
| qwen3-1.7b | 0.7498 | [0.7342, 0.7630] |
| qwen3-0.6b | 0.7457 | [0.7295, 0.7608] |
| pythia-2.8b | 0.7352 | [0.7217, 0.7503] |
| olmo-2-1b | 0.6956 | [0.6792, 0.7105] |
| llama-3.2-3b | 0.6893 | [0.6748, 0.7037] |
| qwen3-8b | 0.6623 | [0.6461, 0.6786] |
| mistral-7b-v0.3 | 0.5472 | [0.5319, 0.5628] |
| **AVERAGE** | **0.7008** | |

## Interpretation

Average F1 = 0.7008, compared to the undemeaned baseline of 0.694.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When LLM outputs are fed back as inputs to subsequent generation, the resulting recursive chains form a dynamical system whose distributional properties evolve with each step.
How this evolution proceeds is a fundamental question that connects to both model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad} and data provenance.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, evidence that LLM text already re-enters training pipelines at scale.
Yet existing detection methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions and obscure qualitative differences: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution while approximately preserving its shape: the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape under standard decoding regimes, while each successive generation compresses the location toward the model's preferred output distribution.
While distributional drift under recursive generation is documented in the model collapse literature \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}, the structured decomposition into monotonically drifting and near-stationary components, and its exploitation for depth classification, has not been previously reported.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice, since instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure this intrinsic mechanism; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The near-stationarity of shape features is consistent with the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constraining distributional shape while allowing location to drift.
Sampling ablation supports this as a tendency rather than a guarantee ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$: ${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation; $t = 1.0$: $-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and prompt-type dependence further modulates the effect (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).

Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints in preliminary experiments (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base, 6-generator LOGO): alignment-imposed length regulation and format constraints compress the distributional variation that DDR exploits.
This restricts current applicability to base models and constitutes the primary scope limitation.
At the document level within base models, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging; the gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ boundary concentrates 86\% of binary errors as false negatives, with larger generators exacerbating this (Mistral-7B error rate 45\% vs.\ Pythia-1B 18\%; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially ($t{=}0.7 \to t{=}1.0$: Qwen3-1.7B F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).
